title: Karmic tail 6-5-17 in the destiny matrix: “Pride”, star sickness and light without an audience

seo.title: Karmic Tail 6-5-17 “Pride”: Meaning in the Destiny Matrix
seo.description: 6-5-17 is the tail of beauty, recognition and pride. A ten-second date check, why everyone with it has the Chariot in the centre, and the Star versus a “star”.

short: 6-5-17 is the karmic tail that popular readings of the destiny matrix call “Pride” — in Russian gordynya, pride as a sin rather than self-respect — and also “Beauty and Vanity”. Its script is a life lived under someone else’s gaze. Everyone has something other people look at: looks, talent, intelligence, taste, flawless correctness. A person with 6-5-17 quietly starts living not by the gift itself but by how it is rated: noticed or not, who is higher, who is lower. The entry into the circle is the Lovers (6) — the wish to please and to be chosen. The circle is held by the Hierophant (5) — a ladder on which any gift turns into rank. On such a ladder a person has only two places: the throne or their knees. At the root stands the Star (17) — a naked woman pouring water from two jugs, with nobody watching her. That is the task of the tail: to shine, not to glitter. So the main question of 6-5-17 is not “how to become more modest” and not “how to win recognition” but how to stop measuring yourself by other people’s eyes. And everyone with 6-5-17 also has a hidden fourth card — the Chariot in the centre of the matrix, the victor with a star on his crown. More on it below.

sections.h2: Do you have the 6-5-17 tail: a ten-second check
paragraphs: The tail depends entirely on one number — the sum of the first three arcana of the matrix. So 6-5-17 can be found without a calculator. Add up three numbers:

ol: **Day arcanum** — the day you were born. If it is over 22, add its digits: 25 → 7, 29 → 11.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If it comes out over 22, add the digits again: 1985 → 23 → 5, 1999 → 28 → 10.

paragraphs: If you get **exactly 17**, you have 6-5-17. No other sum gives this tail, and nothing needs reducing here.

ul: 23.06.2010: 5 + 6 + 3 = 14 → not this one. This is 6-20-14: the same Lovers at the entry, but a different tail.
16.05.1985: 16 + 5 + 5 = 26 → not this one. This is 15-5-8: the same Hierophant in the middle and the same Chariot in the centre, but a different entry and root.

paragraphs: Why it works. A sum of 17 immediately puts D = 17 in the bottom corner of the chart. The centre E is the sum plus the corner: 17 + 17 = 34 → 3 + 4 = 7. The entry of the tail M = D + E = 17 + 7 = 24 → 6, the middle N = D + M = 17 + 6 = 23 → 5. There are no other paths to 6-5-17 — this was checked by running through every date from 1900 to the present day.

There is also a reverse rule, even quicker. The day and month together give at least 2, so the year arcanum of someone with 6-5-17 cannot be more than 15. That means **if you were born in 1942–1948, 1951–1957, 1960–1966, 1970–1975, 1980–1984 or 1990–1993, you do not have the 6-5-17 tail and cannot have it**: the arcanum of these years is between 16 and 22, and there is nothing left for the day and month to add.
The same arithmetic gives facts you will not find in popular readings:

ul: **It is a rare tail.** Among birth dates from 1940–2012, 6-5-17 comes up for about one in 47 (2.1%). That is 18th place out of 26 possible tails.

**It is getting younger.** Among people born in the 1930s it occurred in about one in 520, in the 1960s in one in 69, in the 1990s in one in 42. And among those born since 2000, it is already one in 24, and in this generation it climbs to 12th place. The reason is the small sum. Many twentieth-century years have an arcanum above 15 (1983 → 21), and a sum of 17 is out of reach for them. The years of the 2000s have a small arcanum (2010 → 3), and there is always room for the day and month. Since 1994 there has not been a single year without 6-5-17. The most such dates — 21 each — were in 2001 and 2010.

**A coincidence that is hard to miss.** The tail called “Pride” and “Beauty and Vanity” has become two and a half times more common in the generation that grew up on likes and followers. There is no connection here, only calendar arithmetic. But parents of such children should read the question about children at the end of this article.

**17-5-6 is the same tail.** Some calculators write the tail from the bottom corner to the centre, and then you see the same numbers in reverse order. The roles do not change: the Star in the corner is the root, the Lovers by the centre are the entry. There is no separate 17-5-6 tail: a six in the bottom corner only ever gives 18 or 9 at the entry.

paragraphs: Popular readings explain the name with a legend about a past life. The versions differ. In one, the soul had rare beauty and charm, used them as power, grew proud and humiliated those below. In another, it had high status or great talent, and everything came without effort. Hence the description of this life. The person supposedly feels superior from childhood and expects recognition and help “just because”. Help comes, then there is a setback, and everything has to be won by their own effort. Other readings describe the exact opposite: low self-esteem, hang-ups, dependence on other people’s opinions, an expectation that their talent will be noticed without any attempt to show it. The legend cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about events in the past. But as a metaphor it is accurate. This is how a person lives when their gift has turned into rank.
The words in the name have support in the cards themselves.

ul: **“Beauty”** is in two cards out of three. Waite’s divinatory list for the Lovers begins with the words “attraction, love, beauty”. The figure of the Star, according to Waite, “expresses eternal youth and beauty”, and to prepared minds she appears as “the type of Truth unveiled, glorious in undying beauty”.

**“Pride”** lives in the middle card. About the Hierophant, Waite makes a reservation that reads like a definition of pride. It may so happen, he writes, that “the pontiff forgets the significance of this his symbolic state and acts as if he contained within his proper measures all that his sign signifies”. This is what pride looks like: a person wears what has been given to them and confuses themselves with it.

**Arrogance** also stands in the Star’s divinatory list. In Waite the reversed Star is “arrogance, haughtiness, impotence”. There are no upside-down cards in the matrix, and this is not the meaning of your tail. But it is telling that pride and impotence stand in one line here.

paragraphs: The language itself gives a hint too. The Russian word for vanity, tshcheslavie, is a Church Slavonic calque of the Greek κενοδοξία, kenodoxia, “empty glory”: tshchiy means “empty”, hence tshchetny, “futile”. English has the same idea in vainglory, from the Latin vana gloria. Vanity is glory with nothing inside. And Russians call the conceit of someone who has started being recognised zvyozdnaya bolezn, “star sickness”. The root card of this tail is called exactly that — the Star. The whole script fits into the gap between the two meanings of the word. One star shines while other people’s spotlights are trained on it. The other shines by itself.

And one more detail. Three words from the popular name of the tail stand side by side in an old list of passions. In his book In Aid of the Penitent, St Ignatius (Brianchaninov) lists the eight principal passions, and the last two are vainglory and pride. Under vainglory he writes: “Seeking human glory”, “Attention to the beauty of one’s face, the pleasantness of one’s voice and other qualities of the body”, “Man-pleasing”. Under pride: “Contempt for one’s neighbour. Preferring oneself to everyone.” Beauty, vanity, pride — in two neighbouring items of a nineteenth-century list.

Hence an observation that is rarely made. “Pride”, “vanity”, “humility” are the vocabulary of the church, that is, the vocabulary of the Hierophant, the middle card of the tail. The recipe of popular readings speaks this language too: “success will come through hard work and humility”, “true strength lies in modesty”. Here is the trap. In the ascetic tradition humility is a deep and difficult idea. Retold in everyday terms, it shrinks to “know your place”, and then the person simply moves from the throne to their knees. The ladder stays; only the rung changes. The root card offers a third option: the Star has no throne, no audience and nobody to kneel before.

sections.h2: The gaze, the ladder, the jugs: how the circle works
paragraphs: The three cards of the tail are three attitudes to other people’s gaze. The Lovers: people are looking at me. The Hierophant: who looks down on whom. The Star: nobody is looking, and nobody needs to.

You can see this even in the drawings of Pamela Colman Smith, the artist of Waite’s deck. The fifth and sixth cards are built on one scheme: one figure above, two below. On the fifth, the pontiff sits on a throne, and two ministers kneel before him. On the sixth, a great winged figure above is “pouring down influences”, with a man and a woman below. The seventeenth card breaks this scheme. Above the woman there are only stars, nobody stands between her and the sky, and now she pours the water herself. The comparison is ours; Waite does not make it. But it shows the path of the tail exactly: from “someone stands above me” to “I am the source myself”.

**1. Entry: the Lovers — being seen.** For Waite the sixth card is “in all simplicity the card of human love”: a man and a woman stand “unveiled before each other”. But at the entry of this tail, attraction turns around. What matters is no longer “I am drawn to you” but “I draw people in”. Wen notices an important detail on the card: the man looks at the woman, and the woman looks up at the angel. In this tail love gains a third participant — the one above, whose gaze confirms the choice. Picture a child who more often heard “what a beauty”, “our top student”, “just like his father” than “what do you like?”. They learn a simple formula early: I am loved when I am admired. Wen writes that the Lovers give “a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning”. The paradise of admiration is real: being liked is pleasant, and it works. But on the same card, behind the woman, grows the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, with a serpent coiled around it. In the Book of Genesis the serpent promises: “ye shall be as gods”. The Bible’s first temptation is the temptation of pride, and it is drawn on the entry card of this tail. (This is our observation, not Waite’s reading.)

**2. Mechanism: the Hierophant — the ladder.** In Waite the Hierophant is “the head of the recognized hierarchy”, the outer side of faith, doctrine “when it has passed into the utmost rigidity of expression”. Wen sees in him the pull to conform, to belong to the majority, to have the approval of those in power. “Perhaps,” she writes, “the Seeker is placing too much importance on social and societal approval.” In this tail the Hierophant does one thing: he puts any gift on a ladder. Beauty becomes status, talent becomes a title, intelligence becomes the right to lecture, love becomes “the right match”. And where there is a ladder, there are only two places.

ul: **The throne.** This is pride in the literal sense, Waite’s very pontiff who has forgotten that he only represents something greater. It happens when beauty, abilities or luck that were given to a person, not made by them, start to feel like personal merit.

**The knees.** This is self-abasement. According to Wen, the Hierophant describes a person who relies on another — an authority or an institution — to define for them what is right and what is wrong. In Waite’s divinatory list stand “marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude”, and also “the man to whom the Querent has recourse”. That is a patron. The legend of the popular readings — “they keep getting help, and then comes a setback” — describes the economics of patronage: what is given from above can be taken back from above.

paragraphs: The ladder has one more rule. Wen writes that to conform you have to repress the parts of yourself that are different from others, so the Hierophant is also a card of concealment. On the ladder any admission is a step down: “I don’t know”, “I was wrong”, “help me”. So a person with 6-5-17 hides mistakes, does not ask questions in meetings and does not learn where others can see. St Ignatius wrote down the same thing in the language of the church: among the signs of vainglory he lists “shame at confessing one’s sins” and “hiding them from people”.

**3. Root: the Star — shining without an audience.** In Waite the woman on the seventeenth card is “entirely naked”. Her left knee is on the land, her right foot upon the water, and from two great ewers she pours the Water of Life onto land and sea. The mottoes of the card, according to Waite, are “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”. The simple reading “the Star means hope” he calls “the summary of several tawdry explanations”. To prepared minds, in his words, the figure will appear as Truth unveiled, “pouring on the waters of the soul some part and measure of her priceless possession”. Three details of this scene work against the mechanism of the tail:

ul: **She is naked.** After the Hierophant with his triple crown, triple cross and keys, the root of the tail leaves a person not a single mark of distinction.

**She is on one knee, but not before anyone.** On the fifth card the ministers kneel before the pontiff. On the seventeenth the woman kneels in order to do her work — to pour the water. This is the humility this tail needs: the work matters more than me, not “I am worse than others”.
**Nobody is looking at her.** The only other creature in the scene is a bird on a tree. The water does not belong to the woman; the water passes through her.

paragraphs: Wen adds the main thing. With the Star, guidance “is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within”. For her the Star is a card of generosity, of a person who gives more than they receive. And one more line: “Star personalities master the balance between intelligence and love.” This is exactly the dispute Wen sees on the Lovers card: there the man is the mind and the woman the heart, and a person has to choose between them.

The Star also has a dark detail without which the root of this tail cannot be understood. In Waite’s divinatory list, the upright Star does not begin with hope. First come “loss, theft, privation, abandonment”, and only then “hope and bright prospects”. The Star of this tail is what remains when everything that can be taken has been taken. A naked figure has nothing to steal. So the “loss of status” from the popular legend is, in our reading, not a punishment but the road to the root.

**4. Repetition.** The circle closes when the gaze goes away. The audience got bored, the patron found someone else, beauty began to change with age, someone more talented came along. A person with 6-5-17 falls from the throne to their knees: “I’m nobody.” Or, the other way round, after a long wait they leap from their knees onto the throne: “who are they to judge me?” And then they return to their comfort zone, the centre of the chart, to the Chariot: a new race, a new victory, a new audience. And the circle starts again with the Lovers: “look at me”.

paragraphs: Popular descriptions of 6-5-17 argue with each other. Some write about arrogance, pomposity and a wish to lecture everyone. Others about low self-esteem, hang-ups and dependence on other people’s opinions. Both are right. Psychologists have long distinguished “loud” and “quiet” narcissism: confident superiority and touchy vulnerability. From the outside they are opposites, but inside it is the same dependence on being rated. The tail is not a diagnosis, and it has nothing to do with narcissistic personality disorder. But the mechanism is similar: both the throne and the knees are places on the same ladder.

There is another useful idea. The psychologist Jennifer Crocker described “contingent self-worth”: a sense of your own value that rests on one thing. Among such supports she names appearance, other people’s approval, winning against rivals, academic success and virtue. The three faces of the tail are easy to spot in this list. The Star rests on looks and approval, the Unrecognised Genius on competition and ability, the Righteous One on virtue. Often it is one person in different areas: an unappreciated genius at work, a righteous one at home, a star on social media.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 6-5-17 has the Chariot in the centre
paragraphs: Everyone with the 6-5-17 tail has 7, the Chariot, in the centre of the matrix. This is not a coincidence but arithmetic: the centre is always 17 + 17 = 34 → 7. And the entry of the tail is derived from it: the Lovers are made of the Star and the Chariot (17 + 7 = 24 → 6). Only two tails out of 26 have the Chariot in the centre, 6-5-17 and 15-5-8, and both have the Hierophant in the middle. In this method the centre of the chart is the comfort zone, the state a person returns to when nothing is asked of them.

The comfort zone of 6-5-17 is movement and victory. Wen calls the Chariot a card of conquest, self-control and self-assertion. When the Hierophant’s ladder wobbles, a person with this tail goes off to win: a new degree, a new project, a new body, a new city. And this is useful, because the Chariot is the direct antidote to the knees. Waite describes it precisely: it is “the King in his triumph”, but it typifies “the victory which creates kingship as its natural consequence”, not a kingdom already handed over. And also: “He is not hereditary royalty and he is not priesthood.” The Chariot does not inherit and does not receive the Hierophant’s blessing — it wins. The popular advice to “achieve everything yourself, without anyone’s support” almost repeats what Waite writes about the centre of this tail. This is where the line runs between honest pride and the sin of pride. Being proud of what you have done is the Chariot. Being proud of yourself is the Hierophant’s throne.

But the Chariot has its own trap. Waite stresses that its victory is “above all things triumph in the mind”, that the planes of its conquest are external “and not within himself”, and that “the liberation which he effects may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding”. In the charioteer’s armour Wen sees “a hard encasing over vulnerable human flesh”. Her charioteer likes to appear in control but tends to run from problems or attack them so fiercely as to avoid really facing them. In 6-5-17 this armour often looks like arrogance: someone proud on the outside is often vulnerable on the inside. And a triumph is a parade. A victor in laurels needs an audience, and the Chariot brings the person back under other people’s gaze.

The most beautiful thing in this card is the star. On the charioteer’s crown is an eight-pointed star, and Wen links it directly to the seventeenth card: the same star “recurs here in full bloom”. In her words, “there is a sense that The Star was the source of the charioteer’s divine empowerment”, and the Chariot seems to be “returning from the future”. In the 6-5-17 tail the centre and the root turn out to be two states of one star. On a crown it is an ornament, a sign of victory, and it has to be seen. In the sky it is a source, and it shines even when nobody looks up. The task of the tail in one phrase: **move the star from the crown to the sky.**

Wen has one more remark. If the Chariot and the Star appear together in a spread, it is a sign of great success with “an extraordinary blessing of either fame or fortune”. In the matrix this pair is present for everyone with this tail, in the centre and in the bottom corner. Wen did not write about the matrix, and this is not a promise of fame. But it helps explain why people with 6-5-17 so often feel they are “made to shine”, and why the question of the tail is not “will there be fame” but “whose fame is it, and what for”.

sections.h2: Where else 6, 5, 17 and 7 sound in your chart

ul: **Manipura 7-7-14 — for everyone.** In the chakra table Manipura is built from the centre: the Chariot, the Chariot and Temperance. In this method the hint for this chakra is “status, will, money”, which is exactly the theme of the tail. And in its emotions column stands Temperance, the card of measure.

**The relationship line begins with the Lovers.** Point M is shared by the tail and the relationship line M–R1–R, so for everyone with 6-5-17 the line of love opens with a six. For those with this tail born in 2002, 2011 and 2020, it repeats 6-5-17 entirely.
**The Star sits in Muladhara.** The bottom corner D is the energy column in the first chakra. Everyone with this tail has 17 there.

**The Star on the age scale is the age of 60.** On the age scale the bottom corner governs the span from 60 to 70. In the deck the Star also comes late: according to Wen, it follows the Hanged Man, Death, the Devil and the Tower and means that “the final low point in a situation has passed”. We do not conclude from this that the tail is lived through by sixty. But the root of this tail is drawn in the corner of maturity.

paragraphs: The scenes below are made-up examples, not a description of every person with this tail.

paragraphs.h3: Beauty, the body and the mirror

paragraphs: Popular readings like to say that people with 6-5-17 are especially attractive. But the tail is calculated from the birth date and knows nothing about looks. It describes something else — a person’s relationship with their looks: how much weight they carry in their sense of self and through whose eyes the person sees them.

The script is easy to recognise. Forty-nine photos out of fifty get deleted. The person does not go to the pool, to dance classes or to the gym because “they’ll see I’m out of shape”: pride will not allow being a beginner even in your own body. Age frightens them. In Waite the Star expresses “eternal youth and beauty”, but this is the beauty of Truth, not of skin. The eternal youth of the Star is not about a face.

The strong version is taste and the skill of making things beautiful for others. Design, style, photography, architecture, cosmetology, cooking, the stage. The Star pours water onto someone else’s land. Beauty that is shared works as a gift. Beauty that is displayed works as a rank.

**A partner as a mirror.** What matters is “how we look together”: the partner’s status, looks, education, what friends will say. Both upper cards of the tail are linked to marriage in Waite. The Hierophant’s divinatory list says outright: “marriage, alliance”. And the Lovers, in Waite’s words, were drawn in eighteenth-century decks as a card of married life and called “the symbol of conjugal faith”. In this tail love easily passes through an institution: “the right couple”, “it’s time by thirty”, “what will the parents say”.

**A ladder inside the couple.** Who earns more, who is smarter, who is better-looking. Apologising first is almost impossible: an apology is a step down. A recognisable scene: a quarrel ends not with “I’m sorry” but with a week of cold silence, because “whoever speaks first loses”.

**An ideal instead of a person.** When the Star works not as a compass but as a ruler, the living partner is compared with an image and always loses. Popular compatibility readings write about this tail as a search for the ideal, constant dissatisfaction and the temptation to look for something better on the side. Numbers do not predict affairs. But if a partner is a mirror, every new mirror looks cleaner.
**The version on the knees.** Choosing someone “above yourself” and serving their image. Putting up with neglect because “who am I without him” or “who am I without her”.

The strong version is described by Waite in one phrase: two people “unveiled before each other”. This is love at eye level, without make-up and without roles. The sign is simple: next to this person you can be unattractive, wrong and weak, and they are still there.

This tail has real professional gifts. For Wen the Hierophant is a card of passing on knowledge: teaching, mentoring, explaining are the natural use of this tail. The Star, in her words, is especially favourable for writers, philosophers, researchers and those who give hope back to others. The Chariot brings drive. Public professions, the stage, teaching, the beauty industry, consulting — all of this is within this tail’s reach.
At work this tail has three traps.

ul: **Waiting to be noticed.** One popular reading describes this precisely: the person waits for others to see their talent but does not try to show it. In the language of the cards this is waiting for the Hierophant’s blessing instead of setting out in the Chariot. Picture a designer who has been “finishing the portfolio” for three years: it is not ready until it is perfect.
**A title instead of a craft.** Work is chosen by how it sounds. The higher the position, the harder it is to learn: a lead specialist is ashamed to ask what an intern knows.
**The patron.** A career rests on someone’s support, and when the patron leaves, the very “setback” from the legend happens. The way out is the Chariot: what you have won yourself is what stays.

paragraphs: The same ladder works with money. Money is spent on how a person looks: a brand, a car, a restaurant for the sake of a photo, a loan for the sake of status. The price of their work becomes a verdict on themselves rather than a valuation of the work. Hence two distortions: overpricing out of pride or underpricing out of fear that someone will judge and say “you’re not worth it”.

Popular readings say that children with 6-5-17 can be wilful, stubborn and prone to manipulation, especially if they are indulged in everything. The numbers do not know your childhood. But if the tail resonates, it is worth checking two recognisable scripts. The first is the “show child”, the family’s shop window: loved for top marks, medals, beauty and good manners in front of guests. The second is a strict family that does things “properly”, where your own wishes had to be hidden. In both cases the child learns one thing: your worth depends on how you are rated.

A parent with this tail should look at something else. Has your child become an extension of your status: grades, clubs, competitions, “my child can’t look like that”? The honest question here is this: would you be proud of your child if nobody else could see?

sections.h2: Light or glitter: how to tell them apart

ul: Can you say “I don’t know”, “I was wrong”, “help me” without feeling that you have dropped a rung?
Can you be a beginner in front of everyone — at the first class, in a new team, in a new field?
Are you glad of someone else’s success in your own field? Or does it sting first, with the gladness coming later and with an effort?

paragraphs: **Modesty or self-abasement:**

ul: Do you hide your gift “so they don’t think I’m showing off”?
Do you wait for permission — from a boss, parents, experts — to do what you know how to do?
When someone praises you, can you simply say “thank you”, without “oh, come on, it’s nothing”?

paragraphs: **An ideal or a guillotine:**

ul: Does your ideal show you a direction, or does it forbid any step until the step is flawless?
How many pieces of finished but unshown work are sitting in your drawer?
Would you do this if nobody ever found out?
Does the joy of an achievement last until you tell someone about it? Or does it appear only after the reaction?

sections.h2: What to do with the 6-5-17 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, derived from the logic of the triple — not a ritual and not a promise of results.

ol: **Secret kindness.** Once a week, do something good in a way that nobody finds out about: no stories, no posts and no “just between us”. The Star pours water when nobody is watching. The Gospel advice “let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” is aimed precisely at vanity.

**Three hard phrases.** “I don’t know.” “I was wrong.” “Help me.” Say each of them at least once a week to someone who matters to you. Each phrase is a step off the ladder. And each time it turns out that the floor holds.

**A public beginner.** Take up something you are the worst at: dancing, a language, climbing, drawing. Join a beginners’ group. For 6-5-17 this is the most direct way to stop confusing yourself with your rank.

**“I have” instead of “I am”.** Notice when you equate yourself with your gift: “I’m beautiful”, “I’m clever”, “I’m the best specialist”. Rephrase: “I’ve been given”, “I can”. This is exactly where Waite’s pontiff went wrong: he forgot that he only represents something greater. A gift passes through you, like water through the Star’s jugs.

**Ask a rule whose it is.** For every “that’s how it’s done”, “that isn’t done”, “what will people say”, ask: whose voice is this? Wen sets against the Hierophant a person who decides for themselves what is right and what is wrong. A rule you would choose even today, keep. A rule handed down by someone else’s authority, strip of its veto.

**An ideal is a compass, not a ruler.** When an image of “how it should be” forbids you to act, take one feature from it and take one step now. Show an imperfect portfolio, send an unfinished text, go on a date without a perfect plan. The Star points the way; it does not hand out grades.

**Victory without a parade.** When you achieve something, celebrate quietly first: tell one close person or write it down for yourself. You can post it later, or never. Check whether the joy lasts until the likes arrive. The Chariot’s laurels, yes; the triumphal procession, optional.

**At eye level.** In conversation, notice where you are looking. Down — when you explain, lecture, correct. Up — when you look for approval and nod along. The exercise: where you are strongest, ask another person’s opinion and actually use it. Waite’s Lovers stand “unveiled before each other”, not one above the other.

sections.h2: The strength of 6-5-17: a star that needs no stage
paragraphs: In the lived-through version this tail gives a rare combination. The person has charm and taste (the Lovers). They hold a high standard and know how to pass on knowledge (the Hierophant). They can give hope back to others (the Star) and see things through to the end (the Chariot). Such people make the world more beautiful and other people more confident. This is the teacher after whom students start believing in themselves, not in the teacher. This is the master who holds a standard without contempt for those who do not yet reach it. This is the person people come to when it seems all is lost. According to Wen, the Star is exactly such a counsellor: someone who shares their spirituality with others to restore hope. And Waite calls the Hierophant “the channel of grace”: he does not own it but passes it on, and his hierarchy is only “the reflection of another and greater hierarchic order”.

In the lived-through tail pride does not disappear, but it changes its object. The person is proud of what they have done, not of themselves. This is the pride of the Chariot, which has earned its laurels.

The Star card has a detail that is easy to miss. On the tree behind the woman sits a bird. Wen calls it a scarlet ibis, the sacred bird of Thoth, and writes that the ibis is believed to be a defence against curses of the serpent. The serpent coils around the tree on the entry card of this tail, the Lovers, and promises: “ye shall be as gods”. And at the root sits a bird that protects against this serpent. Our reading: the antidote to the promise “ye shall be as gods” is not “you are nobody” but the simple work of the Star. Pouring water where it is needed.
A star on a crown is there to be seen. A star in the sky shines even when nobody raises their head. 6-5-17 lived through is a person who has moved their star from the crown to the sky.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M. Every sum over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. All the numerical facts in this article come from running through every date from 1900 to the present day: the single sum of 17, the constant centre of 7, frequencies by year and generation, the years without this tail, the match with the relationship line, Manipura 7-7-14.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922), and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Both authors are quoted in their original English. The meanings of reversed cards are given only as information from the books: there are no reversed cards in the matrix.

**The name “Pride” and the past-life legend** come from popular readings of the destiny matrix. The list of passions follows St Ignatius (Brianchaninov), In Aid of the Penitent; the quotations from it are our translation. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails. Assembling the three cards into a script, the reading through the gaze and the ladder, the comparison of the compositions of V, VI and XVII, and the image of a star moved from the crown to the sky are the author’s interpretation.

**Psychology** — Jennifer Crocker’s research on contingent self-worth, the distinction between “loud” and “quiet” narcissism, and the experiments of Carol Dweck and Claudia Mueller on praise (1998). They are given as parallels, not as proof of the method.

This is an esoteric model for self-observation, not a forecast and not a substitute for help from a psychologist. If shame, comparing yourself with others or fear of being judged get in the way of living, that is a reason to talk to a specialist, not to look for an answer in numbers.

paragraphs: For a couple, 6-5-17 brings the wish for a beautiful relationship together with the task of making room for each person’s real dreams. The Lovers at M concern mutual choice and an attractive image of the relationship; the Hierophant at N develops the task through ideas about the “right” way to live; the Star at D asks for support for abilities without comparison to an ideal. This is our reading based on Lisovskaya’s material about couples, rather than a ready-made meaning for the triple in her book.

Imagine a partner wanting to try a creative pursuit that does not fit the family’s picture of serious work. The couple can discuss costs and time, or begin with “That’s not how we do things.” The Hierophant then protects a familiar image of the relationship, while the Star is welcome only as decoration: talent is admired as long as it changes nothing at home. The Lovers face the choice of a real person whose interests may extend beyond the familiar script.

Set a trial period and an affordable budget for one project, dividing household jobs in advance. Afterwards, discuss the experience using criteria chosen by the person leading the project rather than acquaintances’ achievements. The difficulty is replacing support with instruction, or waiting for outside recognition before taking a dream seriously. Shared values can help both people express themselves while allowing a cherished pursuit to mean more than earnings or family approval.

faq.q: What happened in a past life to a person with the 6-5-17 tail?
faq.a: Popular readings say that in a past life the person had beauty and charm or high status and talent, everything came easily, and they grew proud and set themselves above others. Hence the script of this life: help comes and goes, and everything has to be won by their own effort. This is a legend of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events of past lives. It is more useful to read it as a description of what is already visible now — the habit of living by rank and by other people’s gaze. If “everything came for free” rings true for you, the tail’s answer is not to punish yourself. The answer lies in the Chariot — earning things yourself — and in the Star — giving freely.

faq.q: Does 6-5-17 mean that I am an arrogant person?
faq.a: No. The tail does not make anyone arrogant. Popular readings describe the “Unrecognised Genius” form — shyness, self-doubt, waiting to be noticed — as often as arrogance. The tail describes not a character trait but an axis: the habit of measuring yourself and others vertically, who is higher and who is lower. Whether you sit at the top or the bottom is secondary.

faq.q: Is it true that people with 6-5-17 are especially good-looking?
faq.a: The tail is calculated from the birth date and says nothing about appearance. Among those born after 2000, 6-5-17 comes up for about one in 24, and these people are no better-looking than anyone else. The tail describes an attitude to beauty: how much it means to a person, through whose eyes they rate themselves, and what they do with their looks — display them or share them.

Yes. These are the same three numbers of the bottom ray, read in different directions: from the centre to the corner or from the corner to the centre. The roles do not change: the Lovers by the centre are the entry, the Hierophant is the mechanism, the Star in the bottom corner is the root. There is no separate 17-5-6 tail.

faq.q: Are the 6-5-17 tail and the “6-5-17 program” the same thing?
faq.a: Usually yes: popular readings use “karmic program 6-5-17” for the same three numbers of the bottom ray. But such a triple can also occur in other places in the chart, and there it is not a tail. The next question is about this.

faq.q: I found 6-5-17 in my talent line or relationship line. Is that the tail?
faq.a: No. In the talent line the triple 6-5-17 occurs for people born in June who have 11, Strength, in the centre. Their tail is different — 3-22-19 or 21-4-10. In the relationship line 6-5-17 sometimes appears for people with other tails that begin with a six. For those who do have this tail, the relationship line matches it completely only if they were born in 2002, 2011 or 2020. The meaning of the cards in the triple stays the same, but the role is different. The talent line speaks of abilities, the relationship line of how you build closeness, and the tail of a script that repeats by itself.

faq.q: What does 6-5-17 mean in a compatibility matrix?
faq.a: Popular compatibility readings describe it as a chase after an ideal: the partners are dissatisfied with each other and look for something better on the side. A couple’s matrix is calculated from both people’s points, and the tail there describes a script the couple enters together, not each person’s character. By the logic of this article, 6-5-17 in a couple is a “shop window”. The couple lives for how it looks from outside: to parents, friends, social media. And inside, they compete over which of the two is higher. These numbers do not predict affairs. The main risk is different: the two stop seeing each other and see only a reflection. The practices are the same: talk at eye level, celebrate without an audience, be the first to say “I’m sorry”.

With 15-5-8 it shares the Hierophant in the middle and the Chariot in the centre. These are the only two tails with the Chariot in the centre. But the entry of 15-5-8 is the Devil, another card drawn on the “one above two” scheme: the Devil sits above two chained figures. At the root of 15-5-8 is Justice. Put simply, 15-5-8 is about a chain hidden behind a rule: passion, dependence, a family secret. 6-5-17 is about a gift that a rule turns into rank. With 6-17-11 it shares the Lovers at the entry and the Star, but there the Star stands in the middle, that is, in the mechanism. There the ideal itself drives the circle (its popular name is “Wasted Talent”), and Strength stands at the root. In 6-5-17 the Star is not a trap but the way out.

faq.q: Is 6-5-17 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex plays no part in the calculation, and the meaning of the tail does not depend on it. It is easy to fall for the stereotype that this tail holds a woman by her beauty and a man by his status. But this is a stereotype, not arithmetic. A man can be held by his looks, a woman by her position, and either of them by correctness.

The numbers in the matrix do not change; what changes is how the script plays out. Here are the signs of a lived-through tail. You say “I don’t know” and “I was wrong” without a sense of falling. You are a beginner in at least something and are not ashamed of it. You do good that nobody will ever know about. You are glad of other people’s success in your own field. The joy of an achievement does not wait for likes. Your ideal suggests a direction rather than forbidding a step.

faq.q: What should I do if my child has 6-5-17?
faq.a: There are noticeably more such children now than in their parents’ generation: among those born since 2000, about one in 24. The main thing is to praise effort and choices, not looks and talent. There is well-known research on this by the psychologist Carol Dweck. In one experiment, which she ran together with Claudia Mueller, children were praised in different ways after a task: some for intelligence, others for effort. Then they were given hard problems that almost nobody could solve and asked to write to a peer at another school about their results. Among those praised for intelligence, almost four in ten inflated their scores. Among those praised for effort, about one in ten. Praising talent teaches a child to look good; praising effort teaches them to do. So instead of “you’re the prettiest” and “you’re a genius”, say “you worked so hard” and “I like how you came up with that”. Don’t make your child the family’s shop window. Let them be a beginner and lose. And the three hard phrases — “I don’t know”, “I was wrong”, “help me” — say them to your child yourself first.

rows: to please and be chosen: love that looks for an admiring gaze
two people beneath a winged figure
to put the gift on a ladder: who is higher, who is lower
a throne and two figures kneeling
to shine without an audience: to give the gift away rather than wear it
a naked woman pouring water from two jugs
everyone with this tail has it: proving yourself through victories
a star on the victor’s crown

report: The 6-5-17 tail has two portraits, and each rules out the other. Some popular readings describe arrogance and an urge to lecture everyone; others, low self-esteem and the hope that talent will be noticed unprompted. They share a name, “Pride” — pride as a sin, not self-respect — and a legend of a past life where the soul got everything for free and grew proud. Hence, supposedly, the script of this life: help comes, then a setback. The legend cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about past events. But the name does not rest on it. It is written into the cards themselves.

Waite’s caveat about the Hierophant, the middle card of the tail, reads like a definition of pride: “it may so happen that the pontiff forgets the significance of this his symbolic state and acts as if he contained within his proper measures all that his sign signifies”. A person wears what was given and confuses it with themselves.

Language gives a clue too. Russian tshcheslavie, vanity, is a calque of the Greek κενοδοξία, kenodoxia, “empty glory”: glory with nothing inside. And Russians call the conceit of the newly recognised zvyozdnaya bolezn, “star sickness”. The root card of the tail is called just that: the Star. **The whole script fits into the gap between the two meanings of the word.** One star shines while other people’s spotlights are on it. The other shines by itself.

report.h3: A ladder with only two places

report: The three cards of the tail are three attitudes to other people’s gaze. The Lovers: people are looking at me. The Hierophant: who looks down on whom. The Star: nobody is looking, and nobody needs to.

On the Lovers in Waite’s deck, Wen notices a detail: the man looks at the woman, and the woman looks up at the angel. Love gains a third party whose gaze confirms the choice. A child who heard “what a beauty” more often than “what do you like?” learns a formula: I am loved when I am admired. Behind her stand the Tree of Knowledge and the serpent, who in Genesis promises: “ye shall be as gods”. The Bible’s first temptation, the temptation of pride, stands at the entry of the tail. This is our observation, not Waite’s.

The Hierophant, “the head of the recognized hierarchy”, puts every gift on a ladder: beauty becomes status, talent a title, intelligence the right to lecture. “Perhaps,” Wen writes, “the Seeker is placing too much importance on social and societal approval.” The ladder has only two places. The throne is the very pride of the pontiff who forgot that he only represents something greater. The knees are self-abasement and life under a patron: what is given from above is taken back from above. So both portraits are right: **the throne and the knees are rungs of one ladder.**

The ladder has a rule: any admission is a step down. “I don’t know”, “I was wrong”, “help me” sound like a fall. So imperfection is hidden: mistakes are never admitted, and forty-nine photos out of fifty get deleted. A quarrel ends not with “I’m sorry” but with a week of cold silence: whoever speaks first loses. St Ignatius (Brianchaninov) listed among the signs of vainglory “shame at confessing one’s sins” and “hiding them from people”.

“Pride”, “vanity”, “humility” are the vocabulary of the church, that is, of the Hierophant. The recipe of popular readings speaks it too: “success will come through hard work and humility”. In ascetic tradition humility is a deep, difficult idea, but in everyday retelling it shrinks to “know your place”, and the person simply moves from the throne to their knees. **The ladder stays; only the rung changes.**

The root offers a third way. In Waite the woman on the seventeenth card is “entirely naked”, without a single mark of distinction. She is on one knee, but before no one: she kneels to pour the water. This is the humility the tail needs: the work matters more than me, not “I am worse than others”. The water is not hers; it passes through her.

The circle closes when the gaze moves away: the patron finds someone else, someone more talented comes along. The person falls from the throne to their knees: “I’m nobody.” Or leaps from their knees onto the throne: “who are they to judge me?” And then returns to the centre of the matrix.

Everyone with 6-5-17 has the Chariot in the centre, and the tail’s comfort zone is the race: a new degree, a new project, a new city. “He is not hereditary royalty and he is not priesthood,” Waite writes of the charioteer: the Chariot does not wait for a blessing, it wins. Pride in what one has done is the Chariot; pride in oneself is the throne. But a triumph is a parade. A victor needs an audience, and the circle restarts with the Lovers: “look at me”. The price of the circle: fear of ageing and turning out ordinary, years of waiting to be called.

In Waite’s deck the charioteer’s crown bears an eight-pointed star. Wen links it to the seventeenth card: “There is a sense that The Star was the source of the charioteer’s divine empowerment.” The centre and root of the tail are two states of one star. On a crown it is a sign of victory and must be seen. In the sky it is a source and shines with no audience. The task of the tail: **move the star from the crown to the sky.**

report.h3: What is left when everything is taken

report: In Waite’s divinatory list the upright Star does not begin with hope. First come “loss, theft, privation, abandonment”, only then “hope and bright prospects”. A naked figure has nothing to steal. So the setback from the legend is, in our reading, not a punishment but the road to the root.
Practices from the logic of the triple — not a ritual and not a promise of results:

ul: secret kindness: once a week, do something good so that nobody finds out, with no stories and no “just between us”;
three hard phrases: “I don’t know”, “I was wrong”, “help me” — each is a step off the ladder, and each time the floor turns out to hold;
victory without a parade: celebrate quietly first and check whether the joy lasts until the likes arrive.

report: If shame, comparison with others or fear of judgement get in the way of living, that is a reason to talk to a psychologist, not to look for answers in numbers.

report.h3: A teacher whose students believe in themselves

report: Lived through, 6-5-17 is the teacher whose students believe in themselves, not in the teacher. The one people come to when all seems lost. Waite calls the Hierophant “the channel of grace”: he does not own it but passes it on.

On the tree behind the Star in Waite’s deck sits a bird. Wen calls it a scarlet ibis, the sacred bird of Thoth, believed to protect against the serpent’s curses. The serpent promises “ye shall be as gods” at the entry of the tail, and its adversary sits at the root. Our reading: the antidote is not “you are nobody” but the simple work of the Star. Pouring water where it is needed.
